title: Powers of Ten, the World Game, and smart dust
introduction: This week's lecture was about planetary design and computation — seeing the Earth, and everything on and inside it, at scales we cannot normally perceive, so that the systems shaping our world become visible. The speaker used the Eames film Powers of Ten to move from a picnic in Chicago out to the edge of the universe and back down into an atom, then built on it with Buckminster Fuller's World Game and the technology of smart dust.
related_work:
The lecture opened with Powers of Ten, the film made by the Eames office. It starts from a single square metre beside a lake in Chicago, and every ten seconds the field of view expands by a factor of ten — out past the city, the Earth, and the solar system, until it reaches clusters of galaxies millions of light-years away. Then it reverses, returning to Earth and diving into the skin of a hand, through capillaries and cells, and finally into the nucleus of a carbon atom. The whole journey spans forty orders of magnitude — ten to the fortieth — from galactic clusters to an atomic nucleus. Two things about it were stressed. The first is that the film's reference point is human: it begins with a person at a picnic, not with the centre of the Earth, and scales outward to the universe and inward to the body from that one point. The second is that the atom comes back looking like a miniature solar system, a reminder that the micro world mirrors the macro and each atom is a small universe of its own.

For planetary design, the point of all this is to make invisible systems legible. Supply chains and other networks that shape the world are usually unreadable, and the goal is to visualise them so we can understand how they shape us. The lecture used the body as the model: good technology, like a healthy body, is invisible in normal use and only draws attention when it fails — which is exactly the invisible and emergent systems that planetary computation tries to surface.

The second part traced how satellites changed our image of the Earth. They freed us from the flat map, with the Mercator projection's north-south distortions, and let us see the planet whole, as a three-dimensional sphere. They also made it possible to re-scale the world by new measures, drawing countries and continents by energy consumption, non-renewable resources, or population rather than by area. Buckminster Fuller's World Game was the idealistic version of this. Fuller proposed scanning the world's houses and crop yields from orbit, then using computation to route resources where they are needed so that hunger and shortage could be designed away. The game had no winners and no losers; it treated the whole planet as one system working together rather than nations competing — an early, utopian use of computing aimed at planetary-scale human problems.

The final section introduced the exoskeleton, built from multi-scale remote sensing and planetary computation, and focused on smart dust. A mote of smart dust is a chip about one cubic millimetre across, carrying a sensor, a radio, a CPU, and its own power supply, first developed by the military to read its surroundings in real time. In theory you could deploy trillions of these nodes across the ocean floor, the Earth's surface, and even near-Earth space to form a vast sensing network. The applications cut both ways: in war, smart dust scattered from a helicopter and read with a handheld receiver gives instant intelligence about a contact zone; in peace, the same technology is imagined as the Earth's central nervous system, monitoring buildings, infrastructure, and underground mining conditions so that the environment itself can collect and transmit information.
method: My method was to hold onto the film's central move — zooming out and zooming in around a single human point — and use it as a lens on everything else: the World Game as a zoom out to the whole planet, smart dust as a zoom in to the millimetre. That one move kept the lecture from becoming a list of examples.
results_discussion: What stayed with me is the human reference point. Powers of Ten does not start from the Earth or the universe but from a person at a picnic, and that is what gives the forty orders of magnitude their meaning. Planetary design, in this telling, is the same idea scaled up: make the invisible systems around us legible so that a supply chain or a resource flow becomes something you can actually see and act on. Smart dust shows both faces at once — the same technology that sounds utopian when it watches over a building sounds like a weapon when it is scattered over a battlefield, and the lecture did not hide that. That honesty feels closer to what planetary design really is than the World Game's clean optimism.
conclusion_future_work: The takeaway is to keep asking where the human body sits on the scale I am working at. For my own project it is a useful test: does the piece zoom in or zoom out, and what human point does it scale from? I want to carry that question into the projection work.
